narrative:
Over the past quarter century, the Philadelphia City Council has introduced a staggering 8,623 bills, a testament to the city's ongoing efforts to shape its future and address pressing issues. From zoning regulations to transportation infrastructure, these proposals represent a comprehensive attempt to improve the lives of Philadelphians. This data spans from 2000 to 2026, covering two decades of Council activity, and sets the stage for an in-depth examination of the legislative process.

One notable trend is the dominance of certain issue areas, with zoning topping the list at 2,578 bills – nearly a third of all proposals. Planning, infrastructure, and housing also occupy prominent positions, while transportation and finance trail closely behind. Additionally, the data reveals significant fluctuations in bill introductions over time, with 2005, 2012, and 2018 standing out as the most active years, each with over 365 bills introduced. Conversely, the quietest years were 2020 and 2021, with a combined total of only 527 bills.

As Philadelphians delve into this data, they'll discover a 99% pass rate among closed bills – an impressive indicator of the Council's ability to collaborate and produce legislation. However, the sheer volume of bills also underscores the complexities of local governance. By exploring these numbers, citizens can gain valuable insights into how their representatives prioritize issues, identify areas for improvement, and hold elected officials accountable. Open Common Ground empowers Philadelphians with this data, fostering civic engagement, informed decision-making, and a more participatory democracy – one where every voice matters and every proposal has the potential to shape the city's future.
